Saving the Bearded Vulture

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
............a unique way to save and endangered species

Unique Selling Point:
A first for South Africa -- a novel way to save an endangered species

Summary:
The Bearded Vulture is an endangered species with only 1200-1600 adults alive in the world. They occur in Eurasia (Northern Bearded Vulture) and Southern Africa (southern Bearded Vulture). In Europe a unique way of ensuring the survival of teh species has been very successful and this is now attempted for the first time in South Africa.

Further information:
The Bearded Vulture is an endangered species with only 1200-1600 adults alive in the world. They occur in Eurasia (Northern Bearded Vulture) and Southern Africa (southern Bearded Vulture). In South Africa they are also known as the Lammergeier.

Vultures play a crucial role in the circle of life and without vultures eco systems the world over could be compromised.

Now a proactive initiative from the African Bird of Prey Sanctuary outside Pietermaritzburg has launched an innovative programme to save the species.

They have embarked on a project that has in Europe been proven to be very successful and could save the species from extinction.

The vultures always lay two eggs, but only one chick is allowed to survive. The weaker one is pushed out of the nest.

The initiative entails harvesting one egg high in the mountains from nests and then hatching the egg artificially. At the Sanctuary the first Bearded Vulture held in captivity in the southern hemisphere is housed. She is a a non-releasable female called Lesedli.

When the chicks hatch they are raised by means of a puppet and not by humans and spend time with Lesedli. This means, that despite being captive-bred, they can be released back into the wild.

So far, this season has been the most successful on record, despite the problems with Covid and the riots and 8 eggs were harvested in Lesotho and the Drakensberg and 6 chicks have been hatched in this manner. They are growing fast and will form the core of an group that will be released into the wild to save the species from extinction.

There is great footage of eggs being collected, chicks hatching and the pupper feeding the chick and their interaction with Lesedli. The 6 chicks that have hatched are doing well and when we visit the facility can film them the puppet feeding, Lededli and the chicks and other activities at the Centre.

Interviewees:
• Shannon Hoffman – Director of the African Bird of Prey Sanctuary
• Dr Sonja Kruger – KZN Wildlife, and Drakensberg Ecologist,
• Dr Alex Llopis – University of Valentia, Spain. Runs the Vulture Conservation Programme in which 15 European countries participate.

Script:


V/O:
Sphinx is a 15 day old vulture chick and about to enjoy breakfast …... But the grownup feeding him is not a real vulture at all…….. It is a special puppet, created to resemble and adult bird….

The puppet master is Shannon Hoffman who owns the Bird of Prey Sanctuary in KZN near Pietermaritzburg. The chicks she is raising are Southern Bearded Vulture chicks – a species that is on the brink of extinction, with only about 350 of the bids left in the wild.

She has established an extraordinary breeding programme to help save the species. And her life’s journey has prepared her for this.

In the early 2000’s Hoffman spent nearly two years in Dubai, working with birds of prey. In 2006 she founded the Bird of Sanctuary.
Shannon:
So, many of the bids at the facility that I manage here are what we call non-releasable rehabilitation birds. So, they have gone through a formal rehabilitation process and they are just no longer able to go back into the wild
V/O:
In 2012 an extremely rare rescued Bearded Vulture arrived at the facility.
Shannon:
The hope was to patch her up and send her back out into the wild, but she was put into a flight tunnel to check that she could fly and obviously to get her fit. But she walked it. She was not able to fly. So, then a panel of people decided that she was not releasable, and then she ended up living here.
V/O:
They called the bird Lesedi, and she is the first ever Southern Bearded Vulture in captivity. Her arrival piqued Hoffman’s interest in the Bearded Vulture. She became passionate about saving the species and after joining the Bearded Vulture Task Force, a group consisting of several conservation organizations, she started the captive breeding project about 6 years ago.
V/O:
Sonja Kruger of KZN Wildlife is an ecologist and the coordinator of the Bearded Vulture Task Force. She says the birds are also known as Lammergeiers or Lamb Eagles and in the past, this has harmed the species.
Sonja:
So, the main issue really is that they thought they were lamb catchers because every time you saw a bearded vulture it was sitting on a carcass and of course people thought it had killed that animal. And they look more like eagles than vultures, and often when people see a bearded vulture, they its killed that animal.
V/O:
This has led to many birds deliberately being killed on sight. However, the main threat to the species that caused them to become critically endangered, is poisoning.

Hoffman’s initiative entails establishing a genetically diverse population of Bearded Vultures in captivity, and to then release their offspring into the wild. She also realized that Lesedi would be key to the success of the programme.
Mac
And what makes her so special?

Shannon
She is actually pivotal to the whole programme because she has become a surrogate parent for all the chicks that are raised here in captivity.

Mac
So, she is like mother vulture and not mother hen.

Shannon
Absolutely.

Mac
And where do you usually find them in South Africa?

Shannon
So they are in an isolated pocket and the last remnant population is in the Maluti-Drakensberg Mountains. So, it is Lesotho and 3 provinces of South Africa.
V/O:
Hoffman’s extraordinary approach to breeding the birds in captivity is closely aligned to the way in which they breed in the wild.
Shannon:
So, the bearded vultures are an interesting species because like eagles they lay two eggs but only raise one. And then the first chick hatches about a week, six days before the other one. So, the first chick is naturally stronger than the second one and they will outcompete each other a and only one survives.
V/O:
Hoffman obtained permits to harvest the second egg from nests in the wild and raise the chicks in captivity. Harvesting of the extra eggs started in 2015. It is incredibly difficult to access the nests high up in the Drakensberg mountains and Hoffman recruited experienced high-altitude climbers, supported by helicopters. Often the only way to get to nests is to abseil down rock faces.

Once an egg is harvested, it is kept warm in a special container and then transferred to a portable incubator. This is either picked up by helicopter or taken via mountain passes to the sanctuary.
Mac:
When the eggs eventually arrive at the facility what happens then?

Shannon:
We the need to complete that incubation period so they are put into brooders and then when they hatch, it is normally over a 48 hour period, and then from those brooders they are raised for the first 20 days in a heat-controlled environment.
V/O:
In this environment the chicks have limited contact with humans, and that is where the puppet comes in.
Shannon:
There are no parent birds in captivity so what we needed to do was the puppet become the interface between the chick and ourselves. If we raise the chick ourselves the bird is likely to believe that it is a human, and I am putting it very simply, but it is called imprinting and then that brid is not going to be valuable. It does not know it is a bird. It does not know how to breed, it does not know how to socialize.
V/O:
The chicks grow rapidly, and their progress is monitored carefully. At 20 days of age, they are taken out of this heat controlled environment, and placed outside, where they can start to socialize with other chicks. But because they are hard wired to kill each other, they are kept at a distance so that they are able to see and interact but are unable to harm each other.
Shannon:
And then we need a temporary parent which becomes the puppet, and you are feeding and working the puppet when you look after the chicks. And they are put into a rearing enclosure where they have access to Lesedi which is the surrogate parent.

Mac:
And at that age Lesedi does not want to kill them?

Shannon:
No, she might.

Mac:
They are not her chicks,

Shannon:
No, they are not her chicks. So, there is actually a chance that she might kill them. So, we still have to. So, the interaction between the parent and the chick is just visual.

Mac:
So as long as they are seeing Lesedi and almost interacting with her and seeing each other that sort of gives them a natural environment that they would be used to if they were in a nest or living among other raptors.

Shannon:
That is exactly right, Mac. We are faking it, but we are faking it in the best possible way until we can make it.
V/O:
The six chicks that hatched this year have to be weighed regularly.

Chick being weighed

Hildegard is 30 days old.

With the chicks from previous harvests, Hoffman now has a captive-bred population of 13 birds. The offspring of these birds will be released back into the wild. The programme is aptly called “Bred 4 the Wild”.
LINK:
Many people, including some conservationists, are sceptical about an initiative such as this. However, in Europe, a programme with the Northern Bearded Vulture has met with spectacular success.
V/O:
This programme is run by the Vulture Conservation Foundation, which is a collaboration between 40 European organizations and has successfully reintroduced nearly 400 captive-bred Bearded Vultures back into the wild.

And this is exactly what Hoffman hopes to do. She wants to see the offspring of the chicks she and Lesedi raised together one day soar wild and free in the sky above Southern Africa.
